p.src: Now Lin Chong, having killed Wang Lun, stood with his dagger in hand and pointed at the company. “Though I am an officer of the Imperial Guard banished here, today all these heroes have gathered among us. Yet Wang Lun was narrow-minded, jealous of worth and envious of ability, and made excuses to refuse them admission. That is why I killed the wretch in this clash; it was not because I coveted his seat. With my limited breadth of spirit and courage, how could I presume to withstand the imperial armies and cut down the chief villains who corrupt the sovereign’s side? But here is Brother Chao, generous with his wealth in the cause of justice and fully endowed with wisdom and courage. Today, none under heaven can hear his name without submitting to him. Today I put brotherhood above all else and propose that he be made master of the stronghold. What say you?” The others said, “What our leader says is entirely right.” Chao Gai said, “That cannot be. Since ancient times, ‘Even a mighty army does not overrule its master.’ At best, I am merely a newcomer newly arrived from afar. How could I dare take the highest seat at once?” Lin Chong reached forward, pushed Chao Gai into the chief chair, and cried, “Matters have already come to this; pray refuse no longer. If anyone refuses to obey, let Wang Lun serve as his example.” After urging him again and again, they helped Chao Gai into the seat. At Lin Chong’s command, everyone paid homage before the pavilion. Meanwhile, he sent lesser bandits to prepare a feast in the main stronghold, had Wang Lun’s corpse carried away, and dispatched men throughout the front and rear slopes to summon all the junior leaders to the stronghold for their gathering in brotherhood.

p.src: Lin Chong and the others invited Chao Gai to mount a sedan horse, and the whole party proceeded to the main stronghold. On reaching the Hall of Brotherhood, they dismounted and entered the hall together. They escorted “Heavenly King Chao” to the foremost chair in the center and seated him there, then lit a censer of incense in the middle of the hall. Lin Chong stepped forward and said, “I, Lin Chong, am only a coarse, ignorant fellow who knows little beyond the use of spear and staff. I have neither learning nor talent, neither wisdom nor strategy. By heaven’s blessing, so many heroes have gathered at the stronghold today. Our great cause of righteousness now stands clear and can no longer be compared with our former makeshift existence. Since the Learned Master is here, let us ask him to serve as military adviser, control our forces, and command the officers. He must occupy the second seat.” Wu Yong replied, “I am merely a village schoolmaster, without any talent for ordering the realm and relieving the people. Though I have read a little of the military works of Sun and Wu, I have never earned the smallest merit. How could I dare take so high a place?” Lin Chong said, “Matters have already been settled. There is no need for modest refusals.” Wu Yong had no choice but to take the second seat. Lin Chong said, “Master Gongsun, please take the third seat.” Chao Gai said, “That will not do. If there is to be such yielding back and forth, then I, Chao Gai, must give up my seat.” Lin Chong said, “Brother Chao, you are mistaken. Master Gongsun is renowned throughout the rivers and lakes. He excels in warfare, possesses devices unfathomable even to ghosts and gods, and has arts that summon wind and call down rain. Who could equal him?” Gongsun Sheng said, “Though I possess a few minor arts, I have no talent for saving the age. How could I dare take so high a place? You, Leader, should take the seat instead.” Lin Chong said, “Our victory over the enemy this time has already demonstrated the wonders of your arts. We are precisely like the three legs of a tripod: not one can be missing. There is no need for you to decline.” Gongsun Sheng had no choice but to take the third seat. When Lin Chong tried to yield his place again, Chao Gai, Wu Yong, and Gongsun Sheng all refused. All three said, “We have just heard you compare us to the three legs of a tripod, so we dare not disobey your command. Since the three of us occupy the upper seats, if you try to yield your place to anyone else, Chao Gai and the others will have no choice but to withdraw.” The three of them took hold of Lin Chong and made him sit in the fourth seat. Chao Gai said, “Now we must invite Leaders Song and Du to take their seats.” Having seen Wang Lun killed, Du Qian and Song Wan thought, “Our own abilities are slight; how could we rank near these men? We had better earn their goodwill.” They earnestly insisted that Liu Tang take the fifth seat, Ruan Xiao’er the sixth, Ruan Xiaowu the seventh, Ruan Xiaoqi the eighth, Du Qian the ninth, Song Wan the tenth, and Zhu Gui the eleventh.

p.src: Thus the eleven heroes of Liangshan Marsh were established in their seats. Seven or eight hundred men from the front and rear slopes came before the hall to pay homage, then stood in ranks on either side. Chao Gai addressed them: “All of you gathered here, hear me. Today Instructor Lin has helped make me master of the stronghold. The Learned Master Wu shall be military adviser, Master Gongsun shall share command of the troops, and Instructor Lin and the other leaders shall jointly administer the stronghold. Each of you shall retain his former office, manage affairs on the front and rear slopes, and guard the stockades and landing places without allowing any mishap. Every man must exert himself, unite in purpose, and join together in our great cause of righteousness.” He then ordered rooms on both sides put in order to house the families of the two households. Next, the Birthday Gifts they had seized—gold, pearls, and other treasures—together with the gold, silver, money, and valuables on which their own estates had subsisted, were brought out and distributed in the hall to the junior leaders and the many lesser bandits. They slaughtered oxen and horses, offered sacrifices to heaven, earth, and the gods, and celebrated the renewal of their brotherhood. The leaders drank until midnight before dispersing. p.src: Thus, when Lin Chong saw Chao Gai’s magnanimous conduct, his generosity with wealth, his devotion to justice, and the way he had settled every family on the mountain, he suddenly thought of his wife in the capital, whose life or death remained unknown. He therefore confided all that lay in his heart to Chao Gai: “Ever since I came up the mountain, I have wanted to bring my wife here. But seeing Wang Lun’s fickle and treacherous nature, I knew it would be difficult to live under him, and so the matter has been delayed all this time. She has been left stranded in the Eastern Capital, and I do not know whether she is alive or dead.” Chao Gai said, “Since your honored family is in the capital, worthy brother, why do you not fetch them here so that you may be reunited? Write a letter at once. We shall send men down the mountain to travel day and night and bring them here. What could be better?” Lin Chong immediately wrote a letter and sent two trusted lesser bandits from his own retinue down the mountain. Within two months, the men returned to the stronghold and reported, “We went all the way to the residence of Instructor Zhang before the Marshal’s Headquarters in the Eastern Capital. There we heard that your lady, after being pressured by Grand Marshal Gao to accept a marriage, hanged herself and died. She has been dead for half a year. Instructor Zhang, overcome with worry and suspicion, also fell ill and died half a month ago. Only the maid Jin’er remains. She has taken a husband into the household and lives there with him. We questioned the neighbors, and they all gave the same account. Only after learning the truth for certain did we return to report to you, Leader.” On hearing this, tears streamed down Lin Chong’s face. From that time onward, the longing that had weighed on his heart was severed. When Chao Gai and the others heard the news, they sighed in sorrow. Thereafter nothing further occurred in the stronghold. Each day was devoted solely to drilling the troops and preparing to resist the imperial forces.

p.src: Militia commander Huang An led his men aboard the boats and charged toward Golden Sands Beach amid waving banners and battle cries. As they drew near the beach, a mournful, moaning blast suddenly rose over the water. Huang An said, “Is that not the sound of a painted war horn? Divide the boats into two columns for now and moor them in that reed-filled inlet.” Looking out, they saw three boats approaching from far across the water. Each boat carried only five men: four pulled at paired oars, while one stood in the bow. All three were dressed alike, with crimson kerchiefs on their heads and embroidered red silk jackets on their bodies, each holding a barbed boarding hook. Someone among Huang An’s men recognized them and said, “The three men aboard those boats are Ruan the Second, Ruan the Fifth, and Ruan the Seventh.” Huang An ordered, “All of you press forward together and seize those three men!” Forty or fifty boats on either side raised a single battle cry and surged forward to the attack. The men on the three boats gave a shrill whistle, then all turned about at once. Commander Huang flourished the spear in his hand and urged his boat forward, shouting, “Do nothing but kill these bandits! I shall reward you richly.” The three boats fled ahead while the government troops shot arrows after them from the pursuing vessels. The three Ruan brothers went into their cabins, each fetched a piece of blue fox hide, and used it to shield himself from the arrows. The boats behind kept up the pursuit.

p.src: They had pursued them only two or three li along the channel when a small boat flew up from behind Huang An and its men reported, “Stop the pursuit! Every boat from our other column that attacked the inlet has been driven into the water, and all the vessels have been seized.” Huang An demanded, “How did you fall into their hands?” A man in the little boat replied, “As we were sailing, we saw two boats approaching in the distance, each with five men aboard. We joined forces and rushed after them, but before we had chased them three or four li across the water, seven or eight small boats darted out of the narrow channels on every side. Crossbow bolts flew from them like a swarm of locusts. We hastily turned our boats around, but when we reached a narrow channel mouth, we saw some twenty or thirty men on shore stretching a thick bamboo cable between the two banks, barring the waterway. Just as we were about to move forward and examine the cable, they pelted us from the bank with lime jars and stones as thick as raindrops. The government troops had no choice but to abandon their boats, jump into the water, and flee for their lives. When those of us who escaped reached the dry road and looked about, the men and horses that had been on shore had all vanished; even the horses had been led away. The soldiers guarding the horses had all been killed and cast into the water. We found this little boat beside the reed marsh and came straight here to report to you, Commander.”

p.src: When Huang An heard this, he cried out bitterly again and again. He waved the white signal flag, ordering the boats to abandon the pursuit and return together. The fleet had only just turned around and had not yet begun to move when the same three boats appeared astern, now leading more than a dozen others. Each carried only three or five men, who waved red flags and whistled shrilly as they came racing up like the wind. Just as Huang An was about to spread out his boats to meet the attack, a cannon boomed from among the reeds. Huang An looked about and saw red flags filling every quarter. He lost his head in panic. The men on the pursuing boats shouted, “Huang An, leave your head behind before you go!” Huang An had his men row with all their strength toward the reed-lined bank, but forty or fifty small boats darted from the narrow channels on both sides, loosing crossbow bolts as thick as rain. By the time Huang An forced a path through the hail of arrows, only three or four small boats remained with him. Huang An leapt into a swift boat. Looking back, he saw his men jumping one after another into the water with great splashes. Most of those who were dragged away together with their boats were killed. As Huang An fled in the little swift boat, he saw Liu Tang standing aboard a vessel beside the reed marsh. Liu Tang caught Huang An’s boat with a boarding hook, sprang across with a thud, seized him around the waist with one hand, and roared, “Do not struggle!” The other soldiers who knew how to swim were shot dead with arrows in the water. Those who dared not enter the water were all captured alive in their boats. Liu Tang dragged Huang An to the bank. Once ashore, they saw Chao Gai and Gongsun Sheng in the distance, mounted beside the mountain with swords in hand, leading fifty or sixty men and twenty or thirty horses to provide support. Altogether they took one or two hundred prisoners alive. Every captured vessel was collected and moored at the naval stockade south of the mountain. All the chieftains, great and small, returned together to the mountain stronghold. Chao Gai dismounted, entered the Hall of Righteous Assembly, and took his seat. The other chieftains removed their armor and weapons and sat in a circle. They bound the captured Huang An to the general’s pillar. Then they brought out gold, silver, and bolts of satin to reward the underlings. On counting the spoils, they found that more than six hundred fine horses had been taken; this was Lin Chong’s achievement. The victory at the eastern channel was the achievement of Du Qian and Song Wan. The victory at the western channel was the achievement of the three Ruan brothers. The capture of Huang An was Liu Tang’s achievement.

p.src: Let us say no more of how Liangshan Marsh flourished greatly after Chao Gai came to the mountain. Instead, let us tell how the prefect of Jizhou heard the soldiers who had escaped from Huang An’s command recount in detail how Liangshan Marsh had slain the government troops and captured Huang An alive; they also said that the heroes of Liangshan Marsh were extraordinarily valiant and formidable, that no one could approach them, and that capturing them would be difficult; moreover, the waterways were hard to recognize and the inlets and channels confusingly numerous, which was why they had been unable to prevail. On hearing this, the prefect could only lament bitterly. He said to the administrator from the Grand Preceptor’s office, “He Tao first lost a great many men and horses. He alone escaped with his life and returned, but both his ears were cut off. He went home to recover and still has not healed; of the five hundred men who went with him, not one returned. Therefore we next dispatched Training Commissioner Huang An and this prefecture’s bandit-capture officers, leading troops to pursue and seize them, yet they too were all lost. Huang An has been captured alive and taken up the mountain, untold numbers of government soldiers have been killed, and still we cannot win. What are we to do?” The prefect was brooding over his secret anxieties and could devise no solution. Just then an attendant came to report, “A newly appointed official has arrived at the Reception Pavilion by the eastern gate, and an urgent messenger has brought word here.” The prefect hurriedly mounted his horse and rode to the Reception Pavilion outside the eastern gate. As he watched the dust rise, the new official reached the pavilion and dismounted before it. The prefect welcomed him into the pavilion, where they exchanged greetings. The new official took out the Secretariat’s document of replacement and handed it to the prefect. After reading it, the prefect immediately accompanied the new official to the prefectural offices and handed over the official tablets and seals, together with the treasury, funds, grain, and all other matters. A banquet was at once prepared to entertain the new official. The former prefect related in full how powerful the bandits of Liangshan Marsh had become and how they had slain the government troops. When he had finished, the new official’s face turned ashen, and he thought, “Grand Preceptor Cai promoted me to handle this affair, but what a territory and what a prefecture this is! …And without strong troops or valiant generals, how can I possibly capture this band of outlaws? If these rogues should come into the city to ‘borrow’ grain, what could I possibly do? …” The next day, the former prefect packed his clothes and baggage and returned to the Eastern Capital to await punishment, of which no more need be said. Now the new prefect, Prefect Zong, after assuming office, summoned a newly transferred military officer assigned to guard Jizhou. They immediately discussed recruiting soldiers, purchasing horses, gathering fodder, storing grain, and enlisting fierce and courageous laborers and able, resourceful men, all in preparation for capturing the heroes of Liangshan Marsh. On one hand, he submitted a report to the Secretariat, requesting that orders be relayed to the neighboring prefectures and commanderies to combine their strength in the extermination; on the other, he issued documents to the prefecture’s subordinate departments and counties, notifying them of the campaign and ordering the counties to defend their own territories. Of all this, no more need be said.

But Yan Poxi was as fresh and passionate as water, and being only eighteen or nineteen, she was in the very bloom of youth. Song Jiang therefore failed to satisfy her. One day, Song Jiang made the ill-fated mistake of bringing Zhang Wenyuan, a copying clerk in the rear office, to Yan Poxi's house for wine. This Zhang Wenyuan was a fellow clerk of Song Jiang's in the same office. The fellow was known as “Little Zhang the Third” and had fine brows, bright eyes, white teeth, and red lips. He had always loved frequenting the pleasure quarters, drifting about without restraint, and had acquired all the charms and graces of a gallant. Moreover, there was no wind or stringed instrument he could not play. Poxi was a courtesan given to wine and love. The moment she saw Zhang the Third, she was delighted and took a fancy to him. Zhang the Third saw that Poxi was interested and answered her feelings with his eyes. When Song Jiang rose to wash his hands, she even began teasing Zhang the Third with suggestive words. As the common saying goes, “Without wind, the tree does not stir; without a rocking boat, the water does not grow muddy.” Zhang the Third was himself a devotee of wine and women; how could he fail to understand what was happening? Seeing the woman cast amorous glances at him and show such unmistakable affection, he laid the matter to heart. Thereafter, whenever Song Jiang was away, Zhang the Third would go there, pretending that he had merely come in search of him. The woman would keep him there for tea, and as one word led to another, the affair was consummated. Who would have thought that once the woman and Zhang the Third became intimate, their passion would blaze as fiercely as fire? Besides, Zhang the Third was an old hand at such affairs. Have you not heard the old saying about taking neither one thing nor the other along? Song Jiang's one disastrous mistake among a thousand and ten thousand was bringing Zhang the Third to drink at her house, for that was how she first set her eyes on him. Since ancient times it has been said, “Tea brings lovers together, and wine is the go-between of desire.” This affair proved the saying exactly. From the time Yan Poxi took up with Little Zhang the Third, not the least shred of affection for Song Jiang remained in her. Whenever Song Jiang came, she did nothing but wound him with her words and showed him not the slightest warmth. Song Jiang was a true man of valor who gave no thought to women, and so he visited only once every ten days or half a month. Zhang the Third and Poxi became inseparable as glue and lacquer: he went at night and left at dawn. Everyone in the neighborhood knew, and some whisper of it eventually reached Song Jiang's ears. Half believing and half doubting it, Song Jiang thought to himself, “She is no wife chosen for me by my parents. If she has no heart for me, why should I vex myself for no reason? I need only stop going to her door.” From then on, he stayed away for several months. Mother Yan repeatedly sent people to invite him, but Song Jiang always pleaded some business and would not visit. p.src: Now the story divides into two. One day toward evening, Song Jiang came out of the county offices and sat down for tea in the teahouse across the street. Presently he saw a burly man wearing a white Fanyang felt hat and a black-green silk jacket, with leggings and kneeguards below, hemp sandals laced with eight straps, a saber at his waist, and a large bundle on his back. Sweat poured from him like rain, and he panted for breath as he turned his face aside to watch the county offices. Seeing the man behave so suspiciously, Song Jiang hurriedly rose, rushed out of the teahouse, and followed him. After some twenty or thirty paces, the man looked back at Song Jiang but did not recognize him. When Song Jiang saw the man, he found the face somewhat familiar. “Could I have met him somewhere before? …” Yet for the moment he could not recall where. The man studied Song Jiang for a while and also seemed faintly to recognize him. He stopped, fixed his gaze upon Song Jiang, but did not dare ask. Song Jiang thought, “What a strange fellow! Why does he keep staring at me?” But Song Jiang did not dare question him either. Then the man went to a comb-maker's shop by the roadside and asked, “Brother, who is that clerk up ahead?” The master comb-maker replied, “That gentleman is Clerk Song.” The man took up his cudgel-saber, strode before Song Jiang, and bowed deeply, saying, “Do you recognize me, Clerk?” Song Jiang said, “Your face does seem familiar.” The man said, “May we step aside to speak?” Song Jiang thereupon entered a secluded alley with the man. The man said, “We can speak freely in this wineshop.”

p.src: The two men went up to the tavern and chose a secluded private room in which to sit. The man propped his broadsword against the wall, took off his bundle, and tossed it beneath the table. Then he suddenly prostrated himself in obeisance. Song Jiang hurriedly returned the courtesy and said, “May I be so bold as to ask your honorable name?” The man said, “My great benefactor, how can you have forgotten me?” Song Jiang said, “Who are you, brother? You do indeed look somewhat familiar, but I have forgotten.” The man said, “I am Liu Tang, the ‘Red-Haired Demon,’ who once had the honor of meeting you at Constable Chao’s manor and whose life you graciously saved.” Song Jiang was greatly startled when he heard this and said, “Brother, what reckless courage you have! It is fortunate no constable saw you, or you would very nearly have caused serious trouble!” Liu Tang said, “I am so grateful for your great kindness that I would not fear death itself; I came expressly to repay you.” Song Jiang said, “How have Constable Chao and the brothers been lately? Brother, who sent you here?” Liu Tang said, “Chief Chao repeatedly asked me to convey his respects to our great benefactor. Thanks to you, his life was saved, and he is now the supreme chief of Liangshan Marsh. Scholar Wu has become the military adviser, while Gongsun Sheng shares command of the forces. Lin Chong gave him his wholehearted support and killed Wang Lun in the ensuing clash. The stronghold already had Du Qian, Song Wan, and Zhu Gui; together with the seven of us brothers, there are eleven chiefs in all. Seven or eight hundred men have now gathered at the stronghold, and its stores of grain are beyond counting. Mindful only of your great kindness and having no means to repay it, he specially sent Liu Tang with a letter and one hundred taels of gold as thanks to you, Clerk Song, and to the two constables Zhu and Lei.” Liu Tang opened the bundle, took out the letter, and handed it to Song Jiang. After reading it, Song Jiang pulled up the front of his pleated robe and drew out his document pouch. As Song Jiang opened the pouch, Liu Tang took out the gold and placed it on the table. Song Jiang took the letter, wrapped it together with one bar of gold, slipped them into his document pouch, lowered the front of his robe, and said, “Brother, wrap up the rest of this gold just as it was.” He at once called the wine server to bring wine, ordered a large platter of sliced meat, had vegetables, fruit, and other dishes laid out, and told the server to pour wine for Liu Tang. As evening drew on, Liu Tang finished drinking and opened the parcel of gold on the table, intending to take it out. Song Jiang hurriedly stopped him and said, “Brother, listen to me. You seven brothers have only just reached the stronghold and need gold and silver for your expenses. My household has ample means for its livelihood, so leave the money at your stronghold for now. When I lack travel funds, I shall send my brother Song Qing to fetch it. It is not that I mean to keep you at a distance today; I have already accepted one bar from it. Zhu Tong also possesses some family property, so there is no need to give him any. I shall personally explain the kindness intended for him. As for Lei Heng, he does not even know that I warned Constable Chao. Besides, he is addicted to gambling. If he were to take some of it out and gamble, trouble might arise; that would be most unsafe, so on no account must you give him the gold. Brother, I dare not invite you to stay at my home. If someone should recognize you, it would be no laughing matter. The moon will surely be bright tonight, so you can return to the stronghold. Do not linger here. Convey my earnest respects to all the chiefs, and beg them to forgive me for being unable to come and offer my congratulations.” Liu Tang said, “Your great kindness cannot be repaid. My elder brother specially ordered me to bring these modest gifts to you, Clerk Song, as a small token of our devotion. Brother Constable Chao is now a chief, and Military Adviser Wu issues the orders; things are not as they once were. How could I dare take the gold back? I would certainly be punished when I returned to the stronghold.” Song Jiang said, “Since discipline is so strict, I shall write a letter in reply for you to take back. That will suffice.” Liu Tang pleaded insistently with Song Jiang to accept the gift, but Song Jiang would not hear of it. He immediately obtained a sheet of paper, borrowed brush and inkstone from the tavern, wrote a detailed letter in reply, and gave it to Liu Tang to put inside his bundle.

p.src: Liu Tang was a straightforward man. Seeing Song Jiang refuse so firmly, he realized that Song Jiang would not accept the gift and wrapped the gold up again as before. As evening closed in, Liu Tang said, “Since you have written a reply, brother, I shall leave tonight without delay.” Song Jiang said, “Brother, I have had no time to entertain you properly, but our hearts understand each other.” Liu Tang bowed four more times. Song Jiang called the wine server over and said, “This gentleman is leaving one tael of silver here. I shall come tomorrow and settle the account myself.” Liu Tang slung the bundle over his back, took up his broadsword, and followed Song Jiang downstairs. They left the tavern and reached the mouth of the alley. The light was fading; it was the middle of the eighth month, and the full moon was rising. Song Jiang took Liu Tang by the hand and instructed him, “Take care of yourself, brother, and never come here again. There are many constables here; it is no place for dangerous games. I shall escort you no farther. Here we part.” Seeing that the moon shone brightly, Liu Tang lengthened his stride and set off westward, traveling through the night back to Liangshan Marsh.

p.src: Now to return to Song Jiang. After parting from Liu Tang, he walked slowly back to his lodgings, thinking as he went, “It is fortunate no constable saw us. We very nearly brought about a great disaster!” He also thought, “So Chao Gai has indeed turned outlaw, and on such a grand scale.” Before he had rounded two bends, he suddenly heard someone call from behind, “Clerk Song, where have you been? I have not seen you for two whole days.” When Song Jiang turned to look, it was none other than Granny Yan. Because of what now befell, Song Jiang was destined to exchange timidity for daring and a kindly heart for a murderous one.
